The headline that I would pick is rising change throughout the world.

raw_comment:
I noticed that barely any products experienced a price decrease in 2021, and said decreases were extremely minimal. I also noticed that television always saw a decrease in prices relative to the dates on the graph. This is most likely due to the increase popularity of streaming services over the years, and the pandemic pretty much sealed the fate of television. The only products that saw a noticable change in prices at some point of time relative to the graph were televisions, gasoline, and vehicles such as cars and trucks, probably because these are the most used products out of all of the products listed. 

I wonder why the prices of home furniture only rarely experienced decreases? 

My community is very into sports, and it makes sense that the prices for sports equipment went up from late 2020-onward when school reopened and sports were back in session. You've got to do something in response to the increase demand for them. 

This graph showcases the increase and decrease in prices over the course of two years. A good title could be "All Kinds of Products Are Experiencing Price Increases in 2021!"

1. **Chart type**

   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |

| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |
raw_comment:
I noticed that 2021 has a lot of red on the graph compared to 2019-2020 where there is more blue, meaning that the prices have increased in the past year. Additionally, I noticed that the different categories of items are random and don’t have a clear connection to one another.  

I wonder if the increased amounts of red are truly a result of the pandemic? I also wonder how each category is related to one another or were they randomly selected?

This graph is related to me and my community, because all of these items are used on a daily basis, it’s something that most people buy or have bought in the past. In other words, these are all common items that we all pay for, where the increasing prices are affecting everyone.

This graph depicts the price increases of everyday items as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. A catchy headline that I came up with was “Time Flies, Prices on the Rise”.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |
raw_comment: In this graph I notice that the estimated percentiles of prices for this year and next are shown to tranistorily increase by a range of 0-20%.For certain categories such as Gasoline, television and used cars the trend-line is an anomaly. I understand higher demand for gas now that more people are getting back to normal life routines but the price rates proving deflation on television from 2019 until now also makes sense because of the many alternate devices which you would now not necessarily need to purchase television. However I question why now?. Especially when the pandemic first struck and mandates to stay at home were issued I would think that if anything the demand for such items would be when the pandemic first occurred. Cars are now at higher demand so is gas which is unethical for lots of people because transportation is becoming more unaffordable. The rise in gas prices are insane and were very sudden. Prices always change but never to this extreme. This affects the economy significantly because if prices and demand is rising more people won't be able to afford living expenses. Therefore a possible catchy title for this graph could be "Inflation who?".

raw_comment:
This graph shows us the inflation and deflation of the prices presented in certain commonly used products, that have been bought by American citizens with more frequency from the last 2019 period, to the first months of 2022, marking these last ones as an estimate, based on the citizens' consumption. The colors showed, both depicts how high or low the increase of the inflation of some items is; the higher the inflation is presented in some items, such as televisions or gasoline, the red color will be marked, but if there's a decreased on the prices, the blue color it will be.
I wonder if the pandemic was a factor to make the products' prices to rise, during the last periods. Because it's well known that the inflation occurs due to a sustained increase in the price level and also, based and according  to the "Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco" statistics show that this phenomenon was triggered with more agility and that there were interruptions in the supply chains during this period.
Finally, this relates to me, because my community and family are being affected by these pikes in the prices of common used products that we daily need, because we have to pay more and sometimes is hard to us to do so, because our economy is not so high or stable to handle this kind of changes and increases in very short periods of time.

What do you notice?
I noticed that gas had the biggest jump and varied the most in prices, eyeglasses and eye care barely had any change if any and all but eyeglasses and eye care were marked as red in 2021, the one that started as red in 2019 was home furniture, televisions got cheaper and then rose in 2021, and lastly, I noticed that the graph isn't fully labeled so it is not the easiest to clearly read.
What do you wonder?
I wonder why eyeglasses and eye care was able to remain constant unlike the others, how much of an impact COVID had on the inflation rates, and what caused the TV prices to change so much and so often.
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and myself because as a consumer, I am part of the people who are paying these prices and using these different products. How people are able to live and attain the various things are also based on the prices and its availability.
What's going on in this graph? Create a headline.
The graph is showing how much prices have changed over the past couple of years and how it has been affected by COVID. 
"Inflation - How much more are you really paying?"

This could be related to both the shortage of cars being manufactured and the shortage of gasoline, causing the prices to raise. On another note, the prices of televisions experienced a gradual increase, which is much different from the prices of 2019 to early 2020. People were spending a lot more time at home watching shows and movies, so wanting to purchase televisions would make sense.

2. I wonder why the prices of eyeglasses and eye care didn't experience a very noticeable change. I'd assume that people who worked remotely would be using screens all day, so glasses would become more necessary during the day.

3. I am able to make reasonable inferences based on this graph, due to the fact that we were in quarantine last year. The times truly changed drastically, and this change can be observed based on the data presented in the graph.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |
raw_comment:
Q.1 What do you notice?
I notice that there was inflation for the prices of most of items in 2021. When Covid-19 hit around April of 2020, there was a huge decrease in the prices of gasoline. I think that is because people went into lock down and barely drove anywhere and there was too much supplies. Then now into 2021 the demand for gasoline is getting larger as people go out more, so there was an increase in price.
Q.2 What do you wonder?
Why is eyeglasses and eye care a category? Why is there only chicken on here, and no other meats or foods? I wonder why televisions were in a deflation stage for so long before 2021.
Q.3 How does this relate to you and your community?
This relate to my community and me because it is what is happening these days and I can see it around me. We sold our used couch for the same price that we got it for.
Q.4 What's going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graphs' main idea.
In this graph it shows the affects of the Covid-19 pandemic on the prices of items. A catchy title could be, "Covid-19= inflation or Deflation?"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed how inflation began to rapidly increase in 2021. Items like gas and used cars rose drastically. The article mentioned how COVID led to the inflation rate of furniture because people spent more on furniture since everyone was at home. I noticed how home furniture underwent big inflation beginning mid 2020 which was around the height of COVID.
 
What do you wonder?
I wonder if prices like gas and cars have gone up because of lack of resources. The microchip shortage also makes the production of cars difficult so used cars are needed. I also wonder if gas went down a lot during 2020 possibly because of the lack of travel that year.
 
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community because it applies to how our lifestyles affect the prices of different products.

“Inflation has rose at an alarming rate over the past year”

raw_comment:
" A Pricey Pandemic"

I notice that the television prices were drastically decreasing before 2020, but everything else mostly stayed the same, with a few slight changes, as is expected. After the pandemic breakout though, some things started to change more. The gasoline prices decreased suddenly and then went up by a LOT, but TVs started to even out, and everything else evened out.
I wonder why didn't most other things have a more drastic change? I would have expected it, based on what I was hearing and experiencing about some people hoarding supplies, so this is fairly surprising. I also wonder, why is it such an array of random items on this graph? they aren't really related in any way, and there was no big change in the prices of most of them, so what was the point of putting say, chicken on the graph? Why not put on something that was really affected like toilet paper? Anyway, I digress.
I think that this affects me and my community just because these items are things that we all need and live with (I just realized this is how the items are related, at this point it would be pointless to go and change the previous paragraph.) so the price changing affects us all.

raw_comment:
Title: What comes down must go up (at least in terms of prices)


In my opinion this graph is misleading. By just glancing at this graph, one would think that the price of gas and vehicles has gotten higher every month. But because the graph is compared to the previous years prices, this is untrue. While it is true that prices for these things have gone up, because they were so low at the same time the previous year, the are about the same that they were before the pandemic started. This trend is consistent more or less throughout the graph. Also, because the prices are not compared to the previous months, they are not going up month to month, they are only higher compared to last years prices. Also most of these products have reasons other than inflation for their increase in price e.g. televisions because of the perceived shortage of computer chips, gasoline because of the increase in oil prices, and used vehicles because of the shortage of chips to make new vehicle, limiting the supply of new vehicles, thus creating a higher demand for used vehicles. I wounded why the graph is comparing prices from the previous year and not the previous month. I also wonder why these specific products were chosen to be in the graph.

   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

raw_comment:
On this graph, I notice that many prices stayed constant, however things like gasoline, TV's, and cars all rose in price. The inflation is most likely due to Coronavirus. Also, things like technology have decreased in price by a lot. Overall, most things across the graph are rising in price, with the exception of certain things.

I wonder about the role of the government in all of this inflation.

A good title may be "Inflation of The Ages"

raw_comment:
'The Rise and Fall of Prices'

Televisions: I notice that televisions prices have been dropping rapidly. They only recently started to go up slightly. I wonder if this is because you can now watch most of you movies and shows on laptops and phones. Who needs a TV? (I mean personally I like the TV's with big screens but I guess not everyone agrees with me!)

Gasoline: I notice gasoline was kinda up and down staying between -10 and 10 until 2020. Prices then plummeted then suddenly went back up recently. I wonder if this is because people weren't going very many places before covid vaccines were out and now that they are out the people who are actually taking covid seriously (as they should be) are getting vaccinated and then going places again.

Used cars and trucks: I notice that used cars and trucks were slowly going up, then slowly going down, then started to go up, first slowly then very quickly. I wonder why people are suddenly so interested in used cars and trucks.

Eyeglasses and eye care: I notice that eyeglasses and eye care has been going up very slowly. My guess is that the same percentage of people have been needing glasses and that companies are slowly raising their prices.

Chicken: I'm not sure if these are alive chickens or dead chickens. I prefer my chickens to be alive so I'll go with that for now. I notice that chicken prices were pretty much staying the same until recently. Then the price started going up. (continued in comments below)

raw_comment:
Title: Stock Market Rush

I noticed that this graph is showing the inflation of prices for various products including televisions, sports equipment, and eyeglasses. The main thing that I noticed with this graph is that past 2021 the prices of most of these products have increased greatly after in most cases a steady decline or just a small amount of increase occurring each month. What I've also noticed is that the prices of televisions steadily decreased each month (20%) into mid-2020 and then from there began to increase into now, with a 10% increase starting into 2021. Another thing that is prominent in this graph is that the prices of gasoline have been unsteady going up and down over the years and recently began to rise with an over 20% increase. I think that this is due to the changes in fossil fuel digging over the years and that more recently the supply has become scarce causing the prices to rise.    - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

A good headline would be: "Inflation to hurt the nation!"

   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

I also notice that gasoline has noticeable "ups and downs" throughout the graph. Especially in mid-2020. I also notice that as time goes on, every category is increasing.

I wonder if the prices of these items will raise or decrease more or less than 20% in the upcoming years. Why do televisions have more of decrease than the rest and why are used cars and trucks not showing much change.

   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

raw_comment:
This graph is showing the increase and decrease of the price of 7 various items from November of 2018 to May of 2021. I notice that up until January of 2020, Televisions were decreasing by around 20% each month. I also notice that in February and March of 2020 that gasoline (all types) decreased significantly. I think that happened because of COVID and that was when people were in quarantine and didn't use their cars. I notice that eyeglasses and eye care have been continuously increasing in price. I wonder if the headings for the years are for the left side of the heading or the right side. It would make sense if it is the right side because then it would give stuff for 2022 and we haven't gotten there yet. I also wonder what the reasoning for these items is. they seem fairly random because televisions and chicken are not related, and nor are gasoline and home furniture. 
Possible title: Increasing and Decreasing Items

raw_comment:
A1:Inflation of prices seems to be widespread throughout these products and services. Some products are observing severe price inflation like gas and used cars. A lot of recent trends can likely be explained by the Coronavirus pandemic because under the pandemic people were not buying as many products and services because of the stay-at-home order and economic crisis. This is shown especially with the price of gasoline, as it experienced a large amount of deflation in 2020, as people weren’t driving as much to go places. But in 2021, as the mask mandate has lifted, places are reopening, and people are returning to their job sites the demand for gasoline is much greater than in 2020. The same explanation can be used for sports equipment, as the pandemic restricted and decreased the amount of sports activity.
A2:What is making television begin to go up in price again? What is responsible for the recent inflation in home furniture? What part of the pandemic made chicken’s price inflate in 2020? How are lower-income people ever going to be able to afford a car if both used car and truck prices and gas prices are rapidly inflating? 
A3:These are all products we consume, and in some cases rely on. The affordability of products directly affects the living conditions of our residents and their economic situation. If prices continue to inflate for most products it’ll be harder for people to live.
A4:Everything is expensive now? Why is inflation so prevalent in our recovering world?

1. **Chart type**  
   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

|---|---|---|

| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

raw_comment: This graph shows the inflation and deflation rates of items from 2019-2021. Something that I notice is that the biggest increase in inflation was with gasoline. In my community, the gas prices have gone up tremendously in the past 6 months. I wonder what this is exactly from. I can infer that COVID has had a big impact on these rates. Used cars and trucks have also been impacted tremendously by inflation. The automobile industry is getting hit very hard, most likely because of the reopening up of the country. I also noticed that the price of home furniture is starting to go up. The shipping wait for items is so long because everything is so backed up. Most people buy their home furniture off of websites and so the prices are going up because of how long it takes to ship things now. Sports were at a stop at one point because of COVID and now that schools and towns are starting up sports again, inflation has increased. A big question that I have is when these inflation rates are going to go down. COVID has had such a big effect on the economy and inflation and so I wonder if in the future the rates will go down or maybe go back up. This affects my community because the gas rates in my town are very high and, just like the rest of the world, the shipping times for so many online items is so long. A catchy headline is "The U.S. is Inflating".

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

raw_comment:
I noticed that the graph is showing inflation/deflation rates over the span of 12 months. Specifically, when looking at the graph, I noticed that after the start of 2021, there was an increase average price for all different products. I also notice that televisions had a major decrease in average price from the previous months, but once 2021 hit, it took a major turn. 

I wonder why this happened? Was this because of the pandemic ?  Can we expect a major shift in the future ? Also, did the prices of items increase because there is a higher demand or is it because of improved quality of the product? What other factors may have affected this? 

This relates to my community and I because whenever people go to buy items, they wonder to themselves why prices for an item increased or decreased overtime, and if it is still worth buying. Many people may change their life choices based on how much everyday items that they have been using costs. (Does this change the demand for certain items?)

raw_comment:
As COVID-19 has affected supply and demand in many markets, it is possible to discern a pattern across the price changes in this graph. For example, I noticed that the price of sports equipment has gone up recently, which is likely due to the fact that sports teams and recreational sports activities have seen a return to action recently as vaccines have come out. In my community and many other communities, public school sports teams have been brought back. I also noticed that the price of used cars and trucks have gone up as well, which may be due to the fact that more and more people are traveling by car, again due to the release of a COVID-19 vaccine. Also, as businesses come back, so does the demand for used trucks for shipping. Also, the price of home furniture has gone down likely because fewer people are spending time in their homes quarantining. I wonder why the price of televisions has gone up now, though; I can't really see an explanation for that.

Similar effects could have been replicated in sports equipment with less team sports being pursed. |---|---|---|

raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed about this graph was how much gasoline decreased. I understand that because of the virus it is harder to travel, but now that the world is opening up again, I would expect it to shoot back up, especially since many people complain about gas prices. I also wonder why home furniture went down, since more and more people are at home nowadays. My general takeaway however is that most thing did seem to increase over 2020 and 2021. 

I also wonder specifically why televisions have decreased over the pandemic. Aren't people watching more and more TV? I'm sure streaming services and television companies have seen massive profits since the start of the virus. 

This affects me and my community since inflation effects everyone. As prices increase, lower income families or areas will struggle to pay for basic things. Consequently, it will cause a negative effect on the economy.

The demand went down so the price of gas decreased.  
I wonder how the graph would look in the coronavirus pandemic did not happen. I wonder why the price for eye glasses and eye care remained steady.
This relates to my community because my family, friends and I uses the the items listed in the graph everyday.  All of my family wears glasses. Everyday I use a car to get to and from school.
This graph shows the inflation and deflation of items from 2019-2021.
Title:  How Inflation and Deflation Differs Between Everyday Items

raw_comment: In this graph, I notice how out of the seven featured product genres listed on the left side of the graph, televisions are the item that's price decreased the longest amount of time over the last three years. I also notice how gasoline (all types) and used cars and trucks' prices increased the most over the four other products, especially in 2021. However, gasoline prices increased more suddenly than used cars and trucks in 2021. I wonder why gasoline prices decreased exponentially in 2020, and then suddenly increased the same amount in 2021. I believe this graph is showing seven different product groups and a timeline of their inflation and/or deflation over the last three years. My guess for the reason behind the gasoline prices deflation and inflation in 2020 and 2021 is because of COVID-19 regulations lessening in 2021 since 2020's nationwide quarantine. Also, since the last election, the average price per gallon of regular gasoline in the U.S. has increased by 75 cents. This graph relates to me and my community because it affects my families' average spending on these everyday items which affects our financial state. We also have more than one car, so gasoline prices affect our lives every time we have to fill our gas tanks again. Finally, a headline that summarizes this graph is "America's Everyday Item Prices and COVID-19's effect."

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

The two periods with a large increase and decrease in worry about gas inflammation occurred before and after the isolation period of the pandemic, the gas decreased in 2020 and since increased with worry in 2021. There is very little worry changing in the other categories; Glasses and Eye Care, chicken, sports equipment, Home Furniture. Other than gas, television and used cars stand out. Television having a constant decrease in worry from 2019-2020 and small increase going into 2021. Used Cars has had a sudden increase in worry for increased prices, I assume due to lack of availability.

I wonder how the data was gathered to create this graph, if their is consistency in the area of the united states and the consumers that were asked for data. I also wonder what drove them to deciding on these topics.

This graph is showing the change in consumers worry on topics affected by inflammation and increased prices.

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's line moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs show the changes in a sample of consumer product prices, year-to-year (see the Release for an explanation).   

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?" and  "What do you wonder?"  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these graphs and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, October 22 with moderation on Wednesday, October 27.  The topic:  election redistricting based on the 2020 U.S. Census.  Keep noticing and wondering! 

Keep noticing and wondering.

sentence_classifications.image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

raw_comment:
I noticed the change in gas prices from
 2019-2021. The covid pandemic starting in late 2019 led to nation wide quarantine causing a significant drop in usage of vehicles more specifically cars. Thus leading to the dramatic drop in gas prices in November 2020 dropping by 20% in the average gas price compared to the average gas price in 2019. Gas’s November 2021 dark red arrow icon represents an 20 percent increase in average price over November 2020 average price which can be linked to President Biden’s actions as gas prices were below $2 per gallon the day Biden took office. This rise in gas prices caused my parents to begin driving as little as possible to reduce the amount of money spent on gas. The graph represents the inflation which we might not notice which may affect our daily lives more than we think.

raw_comment:
I had first noticed the different shades of the blue and red and the differences of rising prices between specific things throughout the past 3 years. The gasoline spike during 2021 is what most caught my eye because it is strictly dark red which shows the great inflation of gas prices.
I wonder what caused such an increase of prices especially in gasoline, used cars and trucks, and even televisions. Specifically for gasoline, I remember shortly how there was a gas shortage throughout many states, and I wonder if that had anything to do with the increase prices of gas because the less gas there is, the more pricey it could be since everyone uses/needs it. I also wonder if COVID had anything to do with inflation of gas prices because throughout the beginning of 2020, that's when the lockdown happened which people were not allowed to go out meaning that gas was not much needed since people stayed home. But as we go through 2021, that's when lockdown wasn't as strict and everyone wanted to go out which increased the need of gas. 
This relates to myself and my community because these are things that I will end up paying for in the future and as well as now. And if we go on in the same rate then there becomes an even more increase of prices which will most definitely affect our future generations. 
The graph is showing the inflation of prices of certain things throughout the past years and how many of those things have become much more expensive. "Higher Prices, Danger Rises".

raw_comment:
Q1. Something I noticed is that the gasoline prices were at an all time low during the time that the pandemic hit, but rapidly inflated matching the inflation levels of the used vehicles. I think sports equipment was mildly popular, but due to the social distancing and restrictions, people would only buy gear if they could play a sport. 
Q2. I wonder two things why didn’t eyeglasses and eye care take a bigger rise, as I believe staring at a screen is never a good thing, especially fo flours on end? And would computers hav been a better statistic than chicken due to the demands that normally is there, but also with the increased demand with the pandemic?
Q3. I think the the spike in the used cars and trucks began in June 2020, so by that point, people like me were sick of being at home and wanted to maybe travel around. Given COVID-19 was prominent, people in my community didn’t use buses and things like that, so I believe that could be a trend everywhere. My family actually bought a car during the pandemic so we were directly affected by the cost increase due to inflation. I think the chicken price also affects me as my family tends to buy much more chicken than any other meat, so chicken being inflated for a span of over a year recently means we spend more on chicken than we should.
Q4. What’s going on is mainly a drop/deflation then a quick bounce back to inflation. A catchy title could be What Goes Down Comes Back Up.

2. I wonder what caused the decrease in television prices. In addition to this, I wonder why used vehicles went up in price.

4. In this graph, it shows the fluctuations in prices of everyday products. Through the gradation if colors, it is easy to see if the changes were sharp and sudden, or gradual. 
Catch phrase: Inflation, increasing the price of your chicken.

raw_comment:
Headlines: How inflation affects our present and future.

What do you notice? 

I notice how the graph is showing what products would become expensive or be expensive because of inflation. The graph is predicting inflation and deflation rates for 2022. Gasoline, cars, and televisions prices are rising and will be very high by 2022 since inflation is increasing. 

What do you wonder?

I wonder how people predict the inflation rates for 2022 and if we can prevent inflation from happening.

What’s going on in this graph?

The graph is talking about the inflation rates through the years 2019 to 2021. 2022 was also in the graph but they are predicting the inflation rates of 2022.

What impact does this have on you and your community?

This could impact me and my community because if the items get expensive then it will be hard for people to buy the things they want or need.

raw_comment:
U.S. economy still positive for Covid19.
The pandemic has hit the world economy hard. Even the economically most prosperous countries are still not recovering, and this is what we are currently seeing with inflation in the United States. The graph shows how prices have skyrocketed by 10% to 20% in the cost of gasoline, home furniture, some foods such as chicken, sports equipment, and new and used vehicles. The shortage of these products is the leading cause of the price increase due to global supply chains and the lack of people to enter the workforce. 
This economic phenomenon can bring significant consequences for the world economy. The planet continues to show us how vulnerable our economic systems are. Therefore, We should take advantage of this opportunity and this financial crisis to seek alternative solutions that can allow us to move forward.
In the case of the increase in the price of vehicles and gasoline, many governments could be motivating their citizens to purchase electric cars, whose maintenance is much cheaper and environmentally friendly. Moreover, the oil industry should be reduced or ended soon for the benefit of all.
Another essential aspect that we as citizens can consider is to promote local purchasing. Many local food producers, farmer markets, and even the local furniture industry need support. Opting for these and not for imported products instead would be contributing to lessening the impact of the economic crisis.

   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

raw_comment:
I observe the price fluctuation of items (all with different benefits to life) over the past year. I imagine these items were the ones chosen to compared because each one (with the exception of Gasoline and Used cars and trucks because they both relate to the automotive industry) adds to the diverse influx of prices; it shows this was not just inflation in one industry but widely effecting.  From examining the trends, I concluded that Eyeglasses and eye care was the sole data type that did not increase in price over the past year.

Why were Eyeglasses and eye care unaffected by this wide-scale, hybrid, inflation? I wonder why there has been such serious inflation over the past 12 months? Has the supply chain collapse had an impact on the recent lack of goods or high expenses?

My community is greatly affected by these price increases because even though the costs of goods are increasing, income is not. We are now forced to survive on what we have been producing (income) but account for the rise in prices of food, gasoline, furniture, etc. which is very challenging. It is a difficult world we live in and inflation is just one of those imperfections which make life resemble a rollercoaster. 

Understanding the graph represents the alteration of prices over the years, an appropriate title for this graph would be:
The Price's Flight

   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that the graph is demonstrating the inflation of certain products through the usage of color. For instance, the darker the blue, the greater the inflation, and the darker the red, the greater inflation rate. Furthermore,  I also noticed that some of the products have had constant inflation rates over the years, whereas with others, that cannot be said. For example, Gasoline and use cars/trucks have had an exponential increase in the inflation rate in the year 2021. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder if the pandemic had any association whatsoever with the increase or the decrease of the inflation rate of a product? If so, that might explain why gasoline had a major inflation decrease during late 2020 - early 2021, but that doesn't explain why inflation didn't affect televisions during the pandemic.

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because we have to constantly scout out a way to save some money. Therefore, if the cost of essential necessities were to get to out of our budget due to inflation rates, this would affect us in a major way.

What’s going on in this graph?
To my understanding, this graph is demonstrating the inflation rates of certain products from 2019-2021 (nearing 2022) through the usage of color, as well as key that goes along with the colors.

Create a catchy headline that captures the graphs’ main idea.
Should the American Citizens be Concerned about Inflation?

I wonder how we can predict inflation and if we can somehow prevent inflation from happening.

This could impact me and my community because if the items prices start to increase then it will be harder and more expensive for people to buy the items they want and need.

What's going on in this graph? 
The graph is talking about inflation of the item prices through the years of 2019 to 2021. For the year 2022, they are predicting the inflation and deflation rates.

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
There are different ways of representing data using different colors. The darker blue, the negative change. The darker red, the positive change. Also, the graph shows data from 2019, 2020, and 2021. There are multiple different categories such as televisions, gasoline, chicken, ect. Lastly, there is a color-coordinated key showing that the darker the color, the larger the change. 

What do I wonder?
I'm intrigued about why gasoline varied so much. It was mainly decreasing but there were a couple of inflations in consumption about every 9 months. Lastly, there were no huge changes in a decrease or inflation throughout 2020 except for televisions which were at a decrease the entire year. 

How does this relate to me and my community?
The large decrease in gasoline relates to things going on in my life and my community, especially in 2021, because everything got shut down for covid-19 purposes so fewer people were out driving and traveling, resulting in less consumption of fuel. The gasoline graph does show that in the last 3 months of 2020 the consumption of fuel had gone back up. Near the end of 2020, many things started opening back up such as movie theaters and schools. 

What's going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea. 
What is going on in this graph is the many changes in consumption of different products from the end of 2019 to the end of 2021. My title is "The fluctuation of products".

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I notice that the price of televisions has not increased until 2021. On the other hand, the price of gas has been fluctuating but in 2021, it has increased the most. However, eyeglasses and eye care has changed the least in the past few years. The pandemic has definitely affected some of these changes. 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder what is affecting the inflation/deflation rates? I also wonder what this graph will look like in the future and if there will be any more significant changes. Lastly, I wonder what other products have inflated/deflated a lot in the past few years.  
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
This impacts me and my community because I use all of these products and my family can use this graph to determine when prices may inflate or deflate and choose when to buy specific products. Also, our community can advocate for certain products and do more research based on this data. 
4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
In this graph, we see a display of many different products and their inflation or deflation over the past few years. This is displayed with different shades of blue and red.  A catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea would be “Be aware of the Inflation/Deflation Prices”

raw_comment:
What Do I Notice?
I notice that Gasoline has gone up more compared to others. People are using cars, buses, planes, way more than electric cars or bikes to get to the simplest of places. They also drive a lot needing more gas on the way somewhere. Also since more people have been buying used cars, that causes an increase for a need in gas. Also during these times people are trying to stock up with food, which causes a rise in demand. 

I wonder.....why chicken and sports are in this graph. All the others relate to everyday human lives. People sitting on furniture watching television, because of this people need glasses. They are just sitting around all day because they can't go outside.

How it relates to my community?

Well many communities including mine has suffered a lot because of covid. This graph shows the increase of things that people need during these times compared to what they needed back before covid. Something may have risen in demand that people need more of now than what they needed before.

Catchy Phrase/Alternate Title?
Food? Gas? Cars? What has risen and declined during and before covid?

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

|---|---|---|

| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

I wonder what is the name of this kind of graph.
I wonder why was the price of chicken so low in 2019 and 2020 but higher in 2021.

This would have an impact on me and my community because if the prices of gasoline and cars and trucks keep inflating, it'll cost too much for people to pay so it'll be less people traveling with cars and unable to get to places quicker. Chicken is a common food eaten at all homes, restaurants. etc but if the prices of it keep inflating, less people will buy it. 

This data is about the inflation and deflation in prices from the year 2019 to the year we are in now, 2021. A catchy title would be Inflation and Deflation of Prices During 2019-2021.

|---|---|---|

I think what this graph is showing is the price fluctuations in certain things like chicken (still don’t know why thats there) and how they may have gone up in recent times. I think a catchy headline could be “The skews in prices and dates.”

I good headline could be "How prices of high demand products changed over only a few years."

raw_comment:
Headline: "The Dramatic Inflation of Everyday Items: How will it change the future?"

What do you notice?
Prices of common items are going up drastically. For example, televisions, which in 2019 through 2020, had confidently stayed at a lowered cost, until it started to rise. Gasoline, an even more extreme incline, at 2020 rose rapidly towards a dark red, symbolizing a severely inflated price.

What do you wonder?
If all of the prices are going up, how long will it take for the economy to balance, and how will the rising prices affect our lives?

How does this relate to you and your community? 
With the rising prices, our community will continually struggle to keep matching the rising prices, especially with the high unemployment rates. One good aspect of all this, is that with the constant inflation of gasoline, it is pushing us to continue innovation with electric vehicles and healthier energy sources; cleaner energy is required to heal our planet from the pollution we have released and distributed in our atmosphere.

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
I notice that television prices have been on a steady decrease. Gasoline has somewhat been up and down, and recently has begun to increase once again. Used cars are beginning to increase once again, and sports equipment has begun to increase.

What to I wonder?
I wonder why. Some of this is somewhat unusual, like home furniture and sports equipment; why are these important enough to even include?

What impact does it have on you and your community?
Well, an increase in pricing effects everyone, generally. Most of these are goods being consumed by us, so the increase and decrease can either be helpful or unhelpful to the users.

A good title is, "Increasing and Decreasing Prices: Good or Bad?"

raw_comment:
What do I notice? 

I notice that the prices of things like Sports Equipment, Home Furniture, and Eyeglasses/Eye Care have changed, but not dramatically. However, I notice that the prices of Televisions have dramatically dropped over the years, and the prices of Gasoline dropped dramatically, then increased dramatically in recent years. 

What do I wonder? 
I wonder why certain products and services are more subject to being affected by inflation compared to others. What factors into these price changes? 

What impact does this have on you and your community?
The prices of popular products/services like the ones shown in this graph are important to me because they are things I purchase often. Especially things like gasoline. If my family has to spend more on gasoline, then they have less money for other necessary things. It also affects those in my community who have a lower income, and who may not be able to buy products at such a high price. 

What's going on in the graph? Create a catchy title. 
The graph is showing how certain prices have been affected by inflation over a period of time. It also shows that some have been affected much more than others. A catchy title for this graph could be "Inflation Seems to Affect Some Products More Than Others"

raw_comment: I notice that the prices seem have a large deflation in televisions as the years go on. The chicken data hops around a bit from inflation to deflation, but the inflation picks up when we get to 2021. Sports and equipment has a consistent deflation trend until about the end of 2021. This data is affecting my every day life, and I had no clue how until now. This graph is showing the inflation and deflation rates of certain items from the years 2019-2021.

What do I notice?: I notice that this graph shows changes in prices in various categories over the last few years. It seems that the graph predicts prices for 2022 as well. Gasoline shows the highest increase, and eyeglasses and eye care have seen the least increase in prices. I notice that the categories don't really seem to be related to each other in any way, except for gasoline and used vehicles.

What do you wonder?: I wonder why these specific categories of products were chosen. Chicken and eyeglasses don't seem to fit into the same category as all the other products, so I'm interested in why they were added. Were these categories chosen by importance, or by how many were sold?

What impacts does this have on you and your community?: This impacts me because these are all relatively common products my family and I buy. My mom owns a car and buys gasoline, and I recently got new glasses. Because we purchase products like these, we can plan ahead to see what may be more affordable or expensive now.

It uses red to signify an increase in price and blue for a decrease. it shows prices starting in 2019. The products with the most change in prices are televisions, used trucks and cars, and gasoline. A good title for this graph could be "Price Changes Throughout The Years"

   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

What I wonder?
I wonder why eye glasses,chicken,sports equipment and home furniture have the least inflation and have the most deflation? Also why Televisions and gas have a lot of change for deflation? I wonder if covid affected these things to go up? 

How this relates to me:

A possible Title: Inflation and Deflation For Every 12 months For The United States and The  American People.

 In 2019, television prices plummeted the most, while most of the other products had stagnant prices. In 2020, gasoline prices dropped suddenly, but then slowly increased over time. Chicken and used vehicle prices slowly climbed, and all other products were pretty stagnant. In 2021, all products except for eyeglasses and eye care began to rise. Gasoline and used vehicle prices rose the most.

What do you wonder?

I wonder why the prices of television would have dropped the most? Is it because more people were staying indoors during quarantine and already had TVs? I wonder why chicken prices weren't higher either. I figured that people would be stocking up on food which would make chicken high in demand. 

How does this relate to you and your community?

This graph must relate a lot to my community, considering that Louisiana was one of the states hit hardest by the pandemic. I would assume these price changes were pretty consistent with the local economy of Lafayette.

Create a catchy headline.

Saving a Dying Economy

1. **Chart type**  
   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|

Different shades of colors (blue, red and white) mean something different.
Each deflation(shades of blue) and inflation(shades of red) arrow represents 1 month.
Televisions have the most deflations .
Used cars and trucks have the most inflations.
Eyeglasses and eye care has been hardly affected.
What do you wonder?
Why has Eyeglasses and eye care prices been hardly affected?
How can people predict when there will be an inflation, deflation, or no change?
Why start at November 2019, and end at May 2022?
Why does the inflation and deflation rates on cap at 20%?
How does this relate to you and your community?
This affects me because specific things that I use in my daily life is glasses(for my sight), Television(to watch TV), Chicken(to eat with rice), and Home furniture(to decorate the house, and to use). This can affect my community because all these materials(like gasoline, used cars and trucks, sports equipment, etc) are used in everyone’s daily life. So when prices go down, people save less money when buying said material. When prices rise, people will have to save up more money for said material.
Catchy Title:
The Unpredictable but Predictable Inflations and Deflations.

sentence_classifications.image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

raw_comment:
Catchy Headline: Inflation VS. Deflation, Who Will Win?

What do I notice?
I notice that blue arrows represent deflation, and red arrows represent inflation. In 2020, gasoline prices fluctuate. This caught my attention because i know Covid must have been a factor in the fluctuation of these prices. From 2019 to 2021, prices in eyeglasses and eye care only increase. Also, in 2021 prices of television and gasoline decreased.

What do I wonder?
I wonder if the section after 2021 is predictions for 2022. How do they know some prices if we haven't came very close to that year yet?

What impact does this have on you and your community? 
This graph shows the prices of items that are bought regularly in my community. If these prices continue to inflate, my community will struggle with being able to afford it.

raw_comment:
I notice that most of the prices increased between 2020 and 2021, especially the prices of televisions. I’m assuming this is probably due to people over-buying during the pandemic. 
I was wondering why “chicken” is on the graph when everything else is household/technology related. It’s the only food item up there and it’s the only one that really  fluctuates a lot in pricing.  
This relates to me and my community because everything on the graph are common things American  people own/buy. Even a small increase/decrease in price can affect someone’s budgeting 
This graph is showing rising and decreasing prices in things that the average American consumer buys. The reason behind  this graph is to show us how drastic inflation can be and to make us think about whether we should worry or not. If I had to come up with a catchy title for this, I would call it “Recent Fluctuation in Inflation”

raw_comment:
What I noticed?
The red shade represents inflation and the blue shade represents deflation. I noticed that inflation is expected. I also noticed that television prices deflated all through out 2020 to 2021. There's a column for television prices in 2022 which I believe is a prediction of television prices randomly increasing for that year since it's a light shade of red. I also noticed that gasoline prices are constantly increasing and decreasing which makes it pretty unpredictable.

What I wonder?
I wonder why all of these products is prices is expected to increase in 2022? I also wonder if the inflation is because of overpopulation. Are all of these products in high demand because company's don't have the resources to make enough of the products for everyone or are they just taking advantage of us.

What impact does this have on me and my community?
This has a large impact on our community since NYC is expensive and most of the people living around here are lower class and are barely able to make ends. The random inflation in prices will just make every thing more hard on them.

Headline: "The inside scoop on the predicted inflation in the U.S. economy."

   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
I notice that there is data for the months following November 2021 until what seems to be May 2022. This stuck out because we are currently in October 2021 so that might be a prediction for those months. I also notice that this is a different kind of graph than the ones we usually see (pie charts, bar graphs, etc.), This graph uses colors as a scale (Red showing inflation in price and blue showing a decrease in price.). I also noticed that televisions is the only category that stayed at 0 or below in change of price from the start of the graph to the beginning of 2022. Finally, I noticed that most categories increased in price during 2021. 

What do I wonder?
I wonder why these categories were chosen for this graph. 
I wonder if these data sets for the categories are somehow related.
I also wonder how has covid affected the prices for these products.

What impact does this have on you and your community? 
This impacts me and my community because these are some common items that my community and I use a lot. People buy chicken for food, gasoline to fuel their cars, etc. This impacts us because it shows if the prices have been inflated and gives us an idea as to how much we spend on these items. 

What's going in this graph?  Create a catchy title.
The graph shows the inflation or deflation in prices for products from late 2019 to 2021 (maybe even a prediction for 2022).
A catchy title would be "2020 vs 2021 how have the prices for popular items changed?"

raw_comment:
What I notice about this graph is that prices from the year 2019 to 2021 have increased massively. I see this mostly in Used cars and trucks, and gasoline. I find it interesting how both of the most inflated prices on this graph are related to each other. Televisions have also been inflated, but it isn't as extreme as the other two. The rest of items have either stayed the same, or barely changed at all. This tells us that gas, used automobiles, and televisions are in high demand. Unless less people want them, the most likely wont get any lower.

I wonder if the pries of used cars and trucks and gasoline are going to increase even more in 2022. This could be an important factor when it comes to the economy, which could be a bad thing or a good thing. I also wonder why the prices of the other items have barely changed. I find this interesting, because the most expensive items in the graph are ones that have been inflated the most. Which means the more expensive items are the ones in the highest demand.


This relates to me and my community because if the prices of used cars and trucks, gasoline, and other items inflates to much, then nobody will be able to afford them. If less and less people can afford cars, trucks, and gas, then how will they get around? Too much inflation will change the way people spend their money, and maybe could even change the amount of money people make at their job.

However, eyeglasses and eye care prices stayed the same and there isn’t a noticeable change in the prices. The graph also shows that chicken and sport equipment had their prices inflated in 2021. Home furniture also had a small unnoticeable increase.

What do you wonder?
Why were these specific items chosen?
I wonder if this graph shows a prediction for 2022?
If the graph does show a prediction, I wonder if the graph is accurate? (since prices are connected to demands and the demand of people can change easily)

This relates to my community and I because the graph can help people get an overview of the change in prices. This can help many people create a budget plan and know what is expected to get expensive.

Why were Television, gas, truck, eyeglasses, chicken, sports equipment, and home furniture prices picked to reflect inflation and deflation in the American economy? Are these products the most effected by economic fluctuation? Are these products deemed 'most important to Americans'?

Do these fluctuations have to do with covid-19? What impacts did the pandemic, and the economic recession it caused, have on the data? How is it reflected/represented?
